advances: A necessary normal-minimum condition with fixed bodies and sources at every comparison, in the actual vanishing-width uniform-kernel model. The incidence is evaluated at the covariance-shifted source and the offset record comes from the same roofs as the accepted transition Hessian.

proof:
On each fixed positive-width body, nonzero continuous normal makes both ramp kink planes volume-null. A bounded derivative and dominated convergence give the stationary first derivative $\int\psi(q_l)k_l\,d\mu_l=0$. A base tilt by $h_l t a'$ changes the argument exactly by $t k_l$, so actual normal minimization yields the residual inequality after subtraction of that zero linear term.

For a full direction $D=(a',v)$, compare the normal $N_l+h_l tD$ divided by $\Gamma_l(u_l+h_l t v)$, keeping the normalized buffer and width fixed. This division is well-defined for large $l$ and bounded $t$, since the covariance and normal limits are nondegenerate. Expansion of the normalizer on the common compact fiber support gives the changed argument $q_l+t k_l+O(h_l)$ with the stated $k_l$, uniformly on bounded $t$ intervals. The exact infinitesimal normal derivative is the same stationarity equation, by the derivative of this normalizer. The ramp is 1-Lipschitz and the argument error affects it only when $q_l$ is in a fixed bounded interval, since $k_l$ stays bounded. This is a slab of physical width $O(h_l)$ with volume $O(h_l)$, by Fubini along the nonzero continuous normals and the uniform fiber bound. The divided integral error is $O(h_l)$, proving the full-normal residual assertion. On the limiting plane $N\cdot(w-Y)=-b$, so the limit of $k_l$ there is $D\cdot(w-Y)+b u^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v=k_D(w)$.

For bounded $s$, put $G(r,s)=\Psi(r+s)-\Psi(r)-s\psi(r)$. It vanishes outside a bounded $r$ interval and direct integration gives
$$
\int_{-\infty}^qG(r,s)\,dr=B(q,s),\qquad
\int_{\mathbb R}G(r,s)\,dr=0 .
$$
For the second identity use that $J$ is affine with slope one on $[0,\infty)$. Convexity and $0\le\Psi\le1$ give $0\le B(q,s)\le |s|$. The function is jointly continuous on the compactified line times any bounded $s$ interval, since for all such $s$ it vanishes when $q$ is sufficiently far from $[-1,0]$.

Use moving orthonormal normal coordinates on each fiber, with tangential coordinates identified with the limiting plane by rigid motions tending to the identity. Measure along each normal column by its old kernel argument $r=q_l$, so that the volume element divided by $h_l$ is $dr\,d\xi/\|u_l\|$. The integrand is supported in a common bounded $r$ interval, and the tangential domains lie in a common bounded set. Replacing $t k_l$ by its limit at the point of the limiting plane in the column changes the integrand by a quantity tending uniformly to zero on this strip, by the Lipschitz property of the ramp and $|\psi|\le1$. At relative-interior points of a proper limiting section the whole relevant strip is inside the moving fiber for large $l$. This follows from interior membership under Hausdorff convergence of positive convex bodies and from convergence of the coordinate maps. There the full-line residual is zero. Outside a limiting trace the strip is eventually empty, and relative boundaries and lower-dimensional traces are tangentially null. For $d=1$, use the single tangential point with counting measure and ordinary interval columns.

On a compact inner patch of a supporting facet, use the actual near roof $q_l^F$ of c68f502f8530eb6e. That fact's normal-column argument gives the far end uniformly outside the relevant strip. At outside support the occupied interval terminates at its upper roof, giving $+B(q_l^F,t k_D)/\|u_l\|$. At inside support the occupied interval starts at its lower roof, giving $-B(q_l^F,t k_D)/\|u_l\|$ by the zero full-line integral. These computations are uniform on each compact inner patch up to the preceding vanishing replacement error. The bounded tangential strip integrals and the zero area of the relative facet boundary allow patch exhaustion by dominated convergence. More explicitly, the projected strip footprints are eventually contained in any fixed neighborhood of the compact limiting trace, so the omitted outside and boundary neighborhoods have arbitrarily small contribution. The common coarea factors converge to $1/\|u\|$.

All convergence hypotheses of c68f502f8530eb6e hold here, since actual minimization implies local minimization and the bodies, normals, sources, widths, buffers and covariances converge as stipulated. Its common subsequence gives the joint weak graph record of actual $q_l^F$ and the balanced footprint $\chi_l$, with facet area as base marginal and strong capture convergence on compact inner patches. In particular the conditional support is $\Psi(q)=\tau$ outside and $\Psi(q)=1-\tau$ inside. The Bregman integrands are bounded continuous functions of the tangential point and compactified offset, so weak convergence applies on the same patches. Passing the residual inequality to the limit and canceling $1/\|u\|$ gives the signed inequality. It holds for every fixed $t,D$ along this same subsequence because the weak graph limit already applies to all such continuous tests.

For $\Psi(q)=W$ with $0<W<1$ the only offset is $q=W-1$. At $W=0$, for $q\le-1$ the cost is $J(q+s)$ and is nondecreasing in $q$. At $W=1$, for $q\ge0$ it is $J(q+s)-q-1/2-s$, nonincreasing in $q$ because $0\le J'\le1$. Thus $q=W-1$ maximizes the cost also at saturation. Bound all outside costs by their maxima and drop the nonnegative saturated inside costs to obtain the selector inequality.

For finite $q$, $B(q,t k)/t\to[k]_+-\Psi(q)k$ as $t\to+\infty$, since $J$ is zero below $-1$ and affine of slope one above zero. At either infinite offset the cost is identically zero. The bound $B(q,t k)/t\le |k|$ permits dominated convergence after the width limit, giving the stated finite-offset linear inequality. Add the two directions $D$ and $-D$ to obtain its absolute form. An unsaturated selector fixes a finite offset, so $\theta=1$ there.

For the central second coefficient, the 1-Lipschitz derivative $J'=\Psi$ gives $0\le B(q,s)\le s^2/2$. For each finite $q$ away from the two corners, the limit of $[B(q,t k)+B(q,-t k)]/t^2$ is $k^2\mathbf1_{(-1,0)}(q)$, and both infinite offsets give zero. When the corner masses vanish, dominated convergence therefore recovers the covariance inequality with the same $\chi$, by the accepted transition rule. Corner masses may change this limit: the scalar sequence $q_l=-1+1/l$ has balanced footprint one for $l>1$, but its limiting corner $q=-1$ has central second coefficient $k^2/2$. This comparison concerns the order of the two limits and is a scalar calculation.

statement:
In the setting of c68f502f8530eb6e take $N_l=(a_l,u_l)$ to be actual minimizing nonvertical normals for the corresponding finite-width cap with the bodies, source $Y_l=(p_l,y_l)$, normalized buffer $b_l$, width $h_l>0$ and positive definite covariance $\Sigma_l$ held fixed. Normalize $\Gamma_l(u_l)=(u_l^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_lu_l)^{1/2}=1$. Write $\mu_l$ for the sum of the $d$-volumes of the finitely many positive convex fibers. Let
$$
\Psi(q)=(q+1)_+-q_+,\qquad
J(q)=\int_{-\infty}^q\Psi(r)\,dr,\qquad
B(q,s)=J(q+s)-J(q)-\Psi(q)s .
$$
Extend $B$ to $q=\pm\infty$ by zero. At every positive width put $q_l=(N_l\cdot(w-Y_l)+b_l)/h_l$ and $\psi=\Psi'$ almost everywhere. For a base direction $D=(a',0)$ put $k_l=a'\cdot(z-p_l)$. For every real $t$,
$$
\int\psi(q_l)k_l\,d\mu_l=0,\qquad
h_l^{-1}\int\bigl[\Psi(q_l+t k_l)-\Psi(q_l)-t k_l\psi(q_l)\bigr]\,d\mu_l\ge0 .
$$
For $D=(a',v)$ the same inequality holds up to $o(1)$ on bounded $t$ intervals along the convergent sequence, with
$k_l=D\cdot(w-Y_l)-(u_l^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_l v)N_l\cdot(w-Y_l)$.

On a common subsequence with the accepted joint actual roof-offset and transition-footprint record, let $\nu_w$ be the conditional probability of the actual scaled roof argument in $[-\infty,\infty]$ on each limiting supporting facet. Put $\bar Y=Y-b(0,\Sigma u)$, $k_D(w)=D\cdot(w-\bar Y)$ and $dS=d\mathcal H^{d-1}$. Then, simultaneously for all real $t$ and all full directions $D$,
$$
\sum_{\rm out}\int_F\!\int B(q,t k_D(w))\,d\nu_w(q)dS
\ \ge\
\sum_{\rm in}\int_F\!\int B(q,t k_D(w))\,d\nu_w(q)dS .
$$
The support condition is $\Psi(q)=\tau(w)$ outside and $\Psi(q)=1-\tau(w)$ inside, where $\tau$ is the actual outside capture or inside omission selector. Proper cuts and null or empty supports make zero contribution.

For each $t,D$, a consequence is
$$
\sum_{\rm out}\int_F B(\tau-1,t k_D)\,dS
\ \ge\
\sum_{\rm in}\int_{F\cap\{0<\tau<1\}} B(-\tau,t k_D)\,dS.
$$
With $\theta(w)=\nu_w(\mathbb R)$, the same record gives, for every $D$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{\rm out}\int_F\theta([k_D]_+-\tau k_D)\,dS
&\ge\sum_{\rm in}\int_F\theta([k_D]_+-(1-\tau)k_D)\,dS,\\
\sum_{\rm out}\int_F\theta|k_D|\,dS
&\ge\sum_{\rm in}\int_F\theta|k_D|\,dS .
\end{aligned}
$$
Here $\theta=1$ on unsaturated selectors. If the joint offset record gives both ramp corners zero conditional mass almost everywhere, the central second coefficient in the finite-displacement inequality is precisely the accepted transition covariance inequality. At a corner the finite-displacement coefficient and the prelimit balanced endpoint limit can differ.
